items: Genexps only win past a size threshold.
Under a few thousand items the list is faster and simpler.
Chained genexps fuse into one pass — no intermediates.
`sys.getsizeof(g)` reports the object header only.
Pending data is not counted — misleading, but that's the point.
Benchmark with `timeit` at realistic sizes.
Intuition about generator speed is frequently wrong.
Random access is O(n) via `islice` and destructive.
`len()` is unavailable on a generator.
`sum(1 for _ in g)` costs O(n) and consumes it.
Sorting, reversing, multi-pass all force materialization.
I/O-bound streaming is where laziness dominates.
Constant memory over an unbounded file or socket.
A second iteration yields nothing and raises nothing.
The outermost iterable was already evaluated.
So mutating the source later surprises you.

lines: fs = list(lambda: i for i in range(3))
fs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]

items: 3.7+: `StopIteration` inside a generator body converts.
It becomes `RuntimeError: generator raised StopIteration`.
So never call bare `next(inner)` to end a generator.
Use `next(inner, sentinel)` or catch it explicitly.

blocks.title: Bites In Production
items: Un-primed `send()` raises TypeError — advance once first.
`RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`.
Mutating a list while iterating silently skips elements.
A generator object is always truthy — `if g:` tests nothing.
An abandoned generator can hold a file open forever.
Use `with` inside the generator, or `contextlib.closing`.
`return x` does NOT yield x — it ends the generator.
x is hidden in `StopIteration.value` instead.
A paused generator has no visible stack in a traceback.
Errors appear at the consumption site, not the definition.
List comp: indexable, `len` works — small/medium reused data.
Genexp: no index, no `len` — single pass over large data.
`range`: integers only, ideal for numeric loop bounds.

blocks.text: Generator functions also get try/finally cleanup. Iterator classes get introspection and picklability.

caption.text: Part 3 of ITERATORS & GENERATORS. Most Python devs write `yield` for years without ever seeing what it actually does: it freezes a stack frame on the heap and hands the caller a bookmark. This handbook walks the whole iteration model — iter/next mechanics, hand-rolled iterator classes, generator internals (gi_frame, GeneratorExit, PEP 479), lazy pipelines, itertools, and the silent-zero bugs that only show up in production. Save it for the next time `sum(g)` returns 0 and nothing raises.
